Baasha
BAY-uh-shuh
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Basha (H1201); uncertain meaning, possibly "boldness" or "foul-smelling" (a possible derisive nickname recorded in Hebrew). Etymology is contested.

Biblical Definition

Baasha (c. 909 — 886 BC) was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:16-16:7), founder of the second dynastic line in the north (after the brief two-king Nadab line of Jeroboam I), military strongman who came to the throne by assassinating King Nadab during the siege of Gibbethon, and reigned twenty-four years from the city of Tirzah. His coup against Nadab carried out a divine sentence pronounced earlier by the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite against the house of Jeroboam I: "every male of the house of Jeroboam, that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel" (1 Kings 14:10-11) was to be cut off, and Baasha executed this judgment by killing every member of Jeroboam's family (1 Kings 15:29). Yet despite being the instrument of divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam, Baasha promptly continued in Jeroboam's golden-calf apostasy: "And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kings 15:34). His reign was dominated by sustained low-grade warfare against the southern kingdom under King Asa of Judah, especially over the strategic border-town of Ramah (about five miles north of Jerusalem) which Baasha tried to fortify as a base for raiding Judah. Asa responded by hiring the Aramean king Ben-Hadad to attack Israel from the north (1 Kings 15:18-21); Baasha had to abandon his Ramah project; Asa took the building stones Baasha had assembled and used them to fortify the rival Judahite border-towns of Geba and Mizpah. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani then pronounced over Baasha the same kind of judgment Baasha himself had been the instrument of: his whole house would be cut off as Jeroboam's had been (1 Kings 16:1-4). Baasha died in his bed; his son Elah was assassinated in his second year by Zimri; the entire family of Baasha was extinguished in a single coup.

Webster 1828 Definition

Third king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 909-886 BC); founder of the second northern dynasty; assassinated King Nadab; executed divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam I; reigned 24 years; continued in Jeroboam's golden-calf apostasy; warred against Asa of Judah over Ramah.

BAASHA, proper noun. Hebrew Basha (H1201); uncertain meaning, possibly "boldness" or a derisive Hebrew form.

Third king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 909-886 BC); founder of the second northern dynasty.

Assassinated King Nadab during the siege of Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27-28); cut off every male of the house of Jeroboam I in fulfillment of Ahijah the Shilonite's prophecy (1 Kings 15:29 / 14:10-11).

Reigned 24 years from Tirzah; warred against King Asa of Judah; tried to fortify Ramah against Judah but was driven off when Asa hired Ben-Hadad of Aram.

Verdict: 'walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin' (1 Kings 15:34); prophet Jehu son of Hanani pronounced equivalent judgment over Baasha's house (1 Kings 16:1-4).

Key Scripture

1 Kings 15:33-34 — "In the third year of Asa king of Judah began Baasha the son of Ahijah to reign over all Israel in Tirzah, twenty and four years. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin."

1 Kings 15:29 — "And it came to pass, when [Baasha] reigned, that he smote all the house of Jeroboam; he left not to Jeroboam any that breathed, until he had destroyed him, according unto the saying of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite."

1 Kings 16:1-4 — "Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel; and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam, and hast made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me to anger with their sins; Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha..."

Hosea 1:4 — "And the LORD said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel."

Modern Corruption

Baasha is corrupted when his execution of divine judgment against the house of Jeroboam is read as self-justifying merit rather than as the instrumentality it actually was, when his persistent golden-calf apostasy after his coup is overlooked, or when the cyclical pattern of his rise-fall against Jeroboam's house and his own house's later destruction is treated as random political turbulence.

expand to see more

Instrument-as-merit misreading. Baasha carried out the LORD's pronounced judgment against the house of Jeroboam by killing every male of that house. Some readings have treated this as evidence of Baasha's own divine commissioning — he must have been God's chosen instrument, therefore he must have had divine approval. The text rejects this inference at every step. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani delivers a damning judgment against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1-4) precisely on the grounds that Baasha continued the very sin he had been exalted to judge: 'I exalted thee out of the dust... and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam.' Being the instrument of judgment did not absolve Baasha from being judged in turn.

Cyclical-coup as random politics. The pattern across 1 Kings 15-16 is striking: Jeroboam's house is judged by Baasha's coup; Baasha's house is judged by Zimri's coup; Zimri's seven-day reign is judged by Omri's coup. Modern Near-Eastern-history readings sometimes treat this as ordinary ancient-Near-Eastern political instability. The biblical narrator's framing is theological: each successive house began in coup-judgment against the prior house, continued in the same Jeroboamic golden-calf apostasy, and ended in coup-judgment delivered against itself. The pattern is doctrinal cause-and-effect, not random political instability.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Basha (H1201); uncertain meaning, possibly "boldness." Third king of the divided northern kingdom (c. 909-886 BC); founder of the second northern dynasty; reigned 24 years from Tirzah.
